definition: why a hard prohibition rather than weighing the case in front of me

settled:
It does not rest on my present self being worth more. On the ledger everyone weighs the same: future selves and strangers alike, and the present one among them.

It rests on two things that compound.

The first is that I cannot price these costs in the moment. I do not trust that estimate, so I set an absolute instead and take the imprecision of a blunt rule as the cheaper failure.

The second is that harm generally outlasts the self who agreed to it. A choice I make now that harms a later me harms him without his consent, and I have no standing to sign for him.

Neither alone would force a hard rule. A trustworthy estimate could weigh even a terrible downside, and a mild downside would survive an untrustworthy estimate. It is the pair that makes a bright line the right instrument.

It is one of a family of absolutes I adopted on purpose, wherever that same pair turns up.

title: Why That Rule Is A Bright Line
